questions.question: When does the `else` clause of a `try` statement run?
options: Only when an exception was caught by an except clause
Only when the try body completed without raising an exception
Only when no except clause matched
questions.explanation: else runs only if the try body raised nothing. It lets you keep the try body minimal so you don't accidentally catch errors from unrelated code.

questions.question: Why is a bare `except:` considered harmful?
options: It also catches SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt, so things like Ctrl+C stop working
It is a syntax error in Python 3.12
It only catches exceptions derived from ValueError
questions.explanation: A bare except catches BaseException, which includes SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt. Catch Exception at most, ideally something narrower.

questions.question: What does `raise UserNotFound(uid) from exc` do differently from raising without `from`?
options: It discards the original exception entirely
It explicitly sets the original as the direct cause (`__cause__`), shown in the traceback as the direct cause
It converts the new exception into an ExceptionGroup
It suppresses the traceback of the new exception
questions.explanation: raise ... from sets __cause__ and the traceback says the original was the direct cause. Without from, chaining is implicit via __context__ and reads like an accidental error during handling.

questions.question: Given an ExceptionGroup containing a ValueError and an OSError, with separate `except* ValueError` and `except* OSError` clauses, what happens?
options: Only the first matching clause runs, like plain except
A TypeError is raised because except* cannot mix types
Neither runs; ExceptionGroup must be caught by name
Both clauses run, each receiving a group with its matching exceptions
questions.explanation: Unlike plain except, every matching except* clause runs, each receiving a sub-group of the exceptions that match its type.
